impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting judgment as a matter of law that patent claims directed to methods of treating headache using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies were invalid for failure to satisfy the written-description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's JMOL of invalidity for Teva's headache patents covering methods of using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies (the basis for Teva's Ajovy product), reinstating the jury's verdict that Lilly willfully infringed. This is a significant ruling in the ongoing pharmaceutical patent wars over CGRP-pathway migraine treatments.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens patent holders' ability to obtain and enforce genus claims in the biopharmaceutical space, particularly where the specification discloses methods of making the claimed antibodies and at least one working example, supporting broad patent protection for biologics.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies developing competing biologic drugs face increased risk of infringement liability where patent holders hold broad genus claims, potentially limiting generic and biosimilar market entry.

impacts.caseName: Trustees of Columbia University v. Gen Digital Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to methods for detecting anomalous program executions using an emulator and a model of function calls are directed to an abstract idea under Alice step one, and whether the district court erred in awarding damages based on foreign sales of the infringing software.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated a $185 million jury verdict for Columbia, finding the asserted cybersecurity patent claims abstract under Alice step one and remanding for step two analysis. The court also held the district court erred in allowing damages for Norton's foreign sales, and vacated enhanced damages and attorneys' fees that relied on an improper contempt finding.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides defendants with stronger grounds to challenge software and cybersecurity patents under § 101, and limits damages exposure by restricting patent damages to domestic sales absent proof of extraterritorial reach.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders asserting software-related patents face heightened § 101 eligibility challenges and cannot easily recover damages for foreign sales, potentially reducing the value of software patent portfolios significantly.

impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner who has granted an exclusive license but retained the right to sue third parties for infringement independently has sufficient constitutional standing to bring a patent infringement suit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal for lack of standing, holding that a patent owner who retains the right to independently sue for infringement possesses a sufficient exclusionary right to establish Article III standing, even after granting an exclusive license to a third party.
impacts.positiveImplications: Clarifies that patent owners who structure license agreements to retain litigation rights can independently enforce their patents, providing flexibility in patent monetization and licensing structures.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers may face suits from patent owners who have already licensed the patents, complicating defense strategies and potentially exposing defendants to overlapping enforcement actions.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether there was a legally sufficient evidentiary basis to support the jury's finding that each of the four asserted trade secrets was protectable under California law, and whether the inventorship determination for related patents should be reversed when the asserted inventive contribution was generally known information.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the jury's trade secret misappropriation verdict, holding that plaintiffs failed to establish that the asserted trade secrets were protectable because the information was generally known in the field. The court also reversed the patent inventorship correction, finding the alleged inventive contribution consisted of generally known information. The counterfeiting verdict was affirmed.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides defendants with a strong precedent that information generally known in an industry cannot be protected as trade secrets, establishing a meaningful threshold for trade secret protection under California law.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies relying on trade secret protection for product designs and manufacturing processes face a higher evidentiary burden to establish that their claimed secrets are not generally known, potentially weakening trade secret litigation strategies.

impacts.caseName: Insulet Corp. v. EOFlow, Co. Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the three-year statute of limitations under the Defend Trade Secrets Act had expired before Insulet filed suit, given that Insulet had knowledge of the alleged misappropriation more than three years before filing.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the jury's trade secret misappropriation verdict in favor of Insulet, holding that the DTSA's three-year statute of limitations had expired. The court found Insulet knew or should have known of EOFlow's alleged misappropriation of insulin patch pump trade secrets more than three years before filing suit in 2023.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides companies accused of trade secret theft with a robust statute of limitations defense under the DTSA, emphasizing that the clock starts when the plaintiff knows or should know of the misappropriation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret owners must act promptly upon discovering potential misappropriation or risk losing their DTSA claims entirely, creating significant urgency to investigate and litigate within the three-year window.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court correctly granted summary judgment of noninfringement of a multicore processor patent based on extraterritoriality and rejection of the doctrine of equivalents theory, and whether it properly struck certain damages theories.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit partially reversed Intel's summary judgment of noninfringement of VLSI's multicore processor patent, finding that VLSI raised genuine issues of material fact on its doctrine of equivalents theory, while affirming on other grounds. The court remanded for further proceedings, keeping alive a significant patent dispute in the semiconductor industry.
impacts.positiveImplications: Reinforces the viability of doctrine of equivalents claims in semiconductor patent cases, giving patent holders another path to prove infringement when literal infringement is not established.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies face continued uncertainty from DOE infringement theories that may expand the scope of patent claims beyond their literal language, increasing litigation risk and costs.

impacts.caseName: Ollnova Technologies Ltd. v. Ecobee Technologies ULC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a verdict form that asks a single infringement question covering multiple patents, without requiring the jury to identify which patent(s) are infringed, constitutes reversible error requiring a new trial on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated an $11.5 million damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, holding that the verdict form's single question on infringement covering four patents was prejudicially erroneous because it prevented meaningful appellate review. The court also remanded for further proceedings on the § 101 eligibility of the '495 patent under Alice step two.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants benefit from the requirement that verdict forms in multi-patent cases must identify which specific patents are infringed, enabling more targeted appellate review and potentially avoiding overbroad damages awards.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in multi-patent cases face increased procedural complexity in jury trials and risk vacatur of favorable verdicts if verdict forms are not sufficiently granular.

impacts.caseName: AGI SureTrack LLC v. Farmers Edge Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to a relay device for tracking farming operations by collecting data from farming equipment, GPS, and implement profiles are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court erred in finding the case was not exceptional under § 285.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the invalidation of AGI's farming data collection patents as patent-ineligible under § 101, finding the claims directed to the abstract idea of collecting and processing farming data. The court vacated and remanded the district court's finding that the case was not exceptional, potentially opening the door to an attorneys' fees award for the defendant.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides defendants in agricultural technology patent cases a strong precedent for challenging data collection and processing patents under § 101, and opens the possibility of fee-shifting in such cases.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies holding patents on agricultural data systems and precision farming technology face significant eligibility challenges, potentially devaluing patent portfolios in the agtech sector.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the on-sale bar of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. § 102(b) requires that a prior art sale expressly disclose the functionality of the sold device, and whether a Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representative may testify beyond personal knowledge for purposes of summary judgment.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity under the on-sale bar, holding that sales of a prior art device (Hypertech Power Programmer III) more than one year before the patent's priority date invalidated claims for engine controller reprogramming. The court also held that 30(b)(6) witnesses may testify beyond personal knowledge and that computer source code is not hearsay.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants challenging patents can rely on 30(b)(6) testimony from corporate witnesses who lack personal knowledge of historical sales and on source code evidence, broadening the evidentiary tools available for prior art defenses.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face increased vulnerability to on-sale bar challenges even when the functionality of prior art products was not publicly disclosed, as the bar does not require express disclosure of all claimed features in the sale.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform constellations for digital communication systems are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court erred in denying JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated eligibility determinations for certain communication patent claims while affirming eligibility for others, affirmed the jury's infringement finding, and affirmed the damages award. The court found that claims reciting specific technical implementations of non-uniform constellations survived Alice, while more abstract claims required further analysis.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with claims tied to specific technical implementations in communications standards (such as ATSC 3.0) can maintain eligibility even under heightened § 101 scrutiny, supporting enforcement of standards-essential patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies implementing industry communication standards face continued patent infringement exposure, particularly where standards incorporate patented non-uniform constellation designs.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the ITC correctly found that Apple Watch models with blood oxygen measurement features infringed Masimo's patents covering user-worn noninvasive physiological measurement devices, and whether Masimo established a domestic industry.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the ITC's finding that Apple violated Section 337 by importing Apple Watch models that infringed Masimo's blood oxygenation patents, upholding the limited exclusion order barring importation of infringing devices. The court also affirmed the Commission's domestic industry determination.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens the ability of medical device patent holders to use ITC exclusion orders to block importation of consumer electronics products incorporating patented health monitoring technology.
impacts.negativeImplications: Major technology companies integrating health monitoring features into consumer electronics face significant import ban risk from medical device patent holders, potentially requiring product redesigns or licensing agreements.

impacts.caseName: Actelion Pharmaceuticals Ltd v. Mylan Pharmaceuticals Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the claim term 'a pH of 13 or higher' in pharmaceutical composition patents should be measured at the standard temperature convention in the field (25°C), and whether Actelion was barred from asserting infringement under the doctrine of equivalents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's finding of no literal infringement of Actelion's epoprostenol formulation patents, agreeing that 'a pH of 13 or higher' refers to pH measured at the standard 25°C temperature. The court also held Actelion was barred from asserting doctrine of equivalents infringement. This ruling clears the way for Mylan's generic epoprostenol drug.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic pharmaceutical companies benefit from a clear claim construction standard tying pH measurements to field conventions, facilitating design-around strategies for formulation patents and enabling earlier generic market entry.
impacts.negativeImplications: Brand pharmaceutical companies holding formulation patents with measurement-dependent claim terms face narrower claim scope, potentially reducing their ability to block generic competition.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly approved a $125 million class action settlement resolving claims that the federal judiciary overcharged PACER users by using fees to fund expenses unrelated to PACER's operation, and whether incentive awards to class representatives were permissible.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the approval of a $125 million nationwide class action settlement resolving claims that the federal judiciary improperly used PACER fees to fund unrelated court technology systems. The court upheld attorneys' fees awards and incentive awards to the three nonprofit class representatives, finding no abuse of discretion.
impacts.positiveImplications: Businesses and law firms that are heavy PACER users will receive full or substantial reimbursement of excess fees paid during the eight-year class period, providing direct financial recovery.

impacts.caseName: Ascendis Pharma A/S v. BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an ITC respondent that missed the deadline to seek a mandatory stay under 28 U.S.C. § 1659(a)(2) in its original district court declaratory judgment action may obtain a mandatory stay by dismissing and refiling the action.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that an ITC respondent cannot circumvent the statutory deadline for seeking a mandatory stay of parallel district court proceedings by voluntarily dismissing and refiling a declaratory judgment action. BioMarin's strategy of dismissing and refiling to reset the stay deadline was rejected.
impacts.positiveImplications: Protects complainants in parallel ITC and district court proceedings from gamesmanship by respondents seeking to delay district court proceedings through serial refiling of declaratory judgment actions.
impacts.negativeImplications: ITC respondents who miss the 30-day statutory deadline for requesting a mandatory stay of parallel district court proceedings cannot cure the deficiency through refiling, requiring strict deadline compliance.

impacts.caseName: Fortress Iron, LP v. Digger Specialties, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent is invalid for omission of a coinventor when the patent holder acknowledges the coinventor's contribution but is unable to locate the coinventor to add them under 35 U.S.C. § 256, and whether § 256(b) correction is available when the coinventor cannot be found.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that patents were invalid due to the omission of a coinventor (a Chinese manufacturer's employee), even though the patent holder acknowledged the error and attempted correction. The court held that § 256(b) judicial correction was not available when the omitted inventor could not be located, rendering the patents unenforceable.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers can invalidate patents where coinventors from foreign manufacturing partners were omitted, even if the omission was unintentional, creating a powerful defense in cases involving collaborative international development.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop products collaboratively with foreign manufacturers face a significant risk of patent invalidation if foreign coinventors cannot be located for inventorship correction, highlighting the importance of documenting inventive contributions and maintaining contact with all contributors.
